title: The Maronites
hookLine: Lebanon's Syriac church, which says it never broke communion with Rome

cards: A flag with a green tree in the middle. That's the flag of Lebanon, and the tree is a cedar. Walk into a Maronite church, in Beirut or in a suburb far from the Mediterranean, and listen.
The priest prays some of the words of consecration in Syriac, a language close to the one Jesus spoke, and the people answer, often in Arabic.
A family that's been in that parish for generations will tell you something they're proud of: their church says it never broke communion with Rome. Not reunited. Never left.

teach.h: SAINT MARON, A HERMIT IN THE OPEN AIR.
teach.b: The name comes from Saint Maron, a hermit who, tradition says, lived his prayer out in the open air on a hillside in Syria and drew disciples around him. Monks who followed his way became the heart of a church.
Over time, the story goes, that community found its home in the mountains of Lebanon, where steep valleys sheltered monasteries and villages. Then the claim.
Some Eastern Catholic churches tell of a moment when a community, once separated, came into communion with Rome.

teach.h: NO BREAK, THEY SAY, SO NO RETURN.
teach.b: Maronites tell their story differently: there was no such moment, because there was no break. Historians discuss the details; the Maronite church holds this as part of who it is. The Bible loves Lebanon's cedars.

teach.h: GROW UP LIKE THE CEDAR OF LIBANUS.
teach.b: Psalm ninety-one in the Douay-Rheims says, "The just shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow up like the cedar of Libanus." Libanus is Lebanon.

A cedar grows slowly, lives long, smells of resin, and holds its ground on a mountainside. Maronites have taken it as a picture of their own faith: rooted, patient, hard to uproot. Last, a saint who fits the tree.
Saint Charbel was a Maronite monk who spent his last years as a hermit in the mountains, praying in silence, and pilgrims still climb to his monastery.

teach.h: THE JUST SHALL FLOURISH LIKE THE PALM TREE.
teach.b: The church that began with a hermit on a hillside keeps producing hermits on hillsides. And wherever Maronite families have moved, they've carried the cedar with them, sometimes literally, painted over the church door.

how: Maronite Catholics celebrate the Qurbono, their Divine Liturgy, in the West Syriac tradition, with parts in Syriac and the rest in Arabic or the local language; they honor Saint Maron and Saint Charbel, and their parishes stand in countries far from Lebanon.

games.q: you're a Maronite, and a visitor asks when your church came back into communion with Rome. what do you answer?
o: at a reunion council long ago.
it never broke communion, so it never had to come back.
it isn't in communion with Rome.
games.why: Maronites say there was no break, so there was nothing to reunite. historians discuss the details; the church holds this as part of who it is.

practice: Sit tall, like a tree with deep roots, and picture a mountainside of cedars above the sea, then the towns below: crowded streets, families who have lived through hard years, churches and mosques side by side.

Hold the place with respect. If you pray, pray for Lebanon and everyone who lives there, perhaps with the psalm's line, the just shall flourish like the palm tree; if you don't, wish its people a peaceful night.

wordCard.voice: The Maronites. A Syriac Catholic church rooted in Lebanon, named for the hermit Saint Maron, which says it never broke communion with Rome. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: cedar, the tree of Lebanon that the psalms use for the just.

carryVoice: Your line: the cedars. Like the tree, slow, rooted, and hard to uproot. See you tomorrow.
